blocks.text: Overview

Week 3 turns Kirchhoff’s current law (KCL), Kirchhoff’s voltage law (KVL), and Ohm’s law into two systematic ways to solve circuits that are difficult to reduce by series and parallel combinations. First identify the circuit’s structure, then solve for node voltages or mesh currents, including the constraints imposed by dependent sources.
Learning outcomes

items: Identify planar circuits, nodes, essential nodes, branches, essential branches, loops, and meshes (Nilsson 4.1).
Apply the node-voltage method with independent and dependent sources, including known node voltages and supernodes (Nilsson 4.2–4.4).
Apply the mesh-current method to planar circuits with independent and dependent sources, including known mesh currents and supermeshes (Nilsson 4.5–4.7).

blocks.text: Topic 1: Circuit analysis terminology

Topology tells you which points share a voltage and which elements share a current. Treat an uninterrupted ideal wire as one node, regardless of how many bends or labeled points it contains. A planar circuit can be redrawn on a flat plane without branch crossings; a crossing in one drawing does not by itself make the circuit nonplanar.

rows: A connection of two or more elements; all points on the same ideal wire have one potential.
A node where three or more elements meet.
A trace through connected elements without repeating an element.
An element path between nodes; use individual elements when counting branches here.
A path between essential nodes that passes through no other essential node; it may contain several series elements.
A closed path whose final node is its starting node.
A loop containing no other loop in a planar drawing.
A circuit that admits a drawing with no crossing branches.

blocks.text: Here $n$ counts all nodes, $b$ counts all element branches, $n_e$ counts essential nodes, $b_e$ counts essential branches, and $M$ counts independent loops (meshes for a connected planar drawing). These are structural counts. Known current sources add current constraints, so do not count their currents as new unknowns or blindly use the structural mesh count as the number of ordinary KVL equations. Only $n-1$ KCL equations are independent because adding the equations for all nodes gives zero.

blocks.answer: 7 nodes ($a$–$g$); 4 essential nodes ($b,c,e,g$); 10 branches; 7 essential branches; 4 meshes.

Find the nodes, essential nodes, branches, essential branches and meshes.

```schematic
V1 0,6 -> 0,3 "$v_1$"
V2 0,3 -> 0,0 "$v_2$"
R1 0,6 -> 4,6 "$R_1$"
R5 4,6 -> 4,3 "$R_5$"
R2 0,3 -> 2,3 "$R_2$"
R3 2,3 -> 4,3 "$R_3$"
R6 4,3 -> 4,0 "$R_6$"
R4 0,0 -> 4,0 "$R_4$"
wire 4,6 -> 9,6
wire 4,0 -> 9,0
R7 6.5,6 -> 6.5,0 "$R_7$"
I1 9,0 -> 9,6 "$I$"
```

steps.explanation: The distinct nodes are a, b, c, d, e, f, g. Each of the ten listed elements forms one branch.
These four nodes each connect at least three elements. Nodes a, d, f each connect only two.
The essential branches are c–a–b; c–f–g; c–d–e; b–e; e–g; and the two distinct b–g branches through R7 and I.
The meshes use (v1,R1,R5,R3,R2), (v2,R4,R6,R3,R2), (R5,R6,R7), and (R7,I). The loop through R5,R6,I encloses a smaller loop and is not a mesh.

blocks.title: Reading a circuit's structure (Lecture 3)

blocks.text: A line crossing without a junction is not a connection. Keep parallel branches separate when counting; two elements with the same endpoints still form two branches. A mesh depends on a planar drawing, whereas a node depends on electrical connectivity.
Collapse only the nonessential nodes when counting essential branches. Verify your mesh count with both $b-n+1$ and $b_e-n_e+1$.
Topic 2: Node-voltage method

Use node voltages when you want a compact description of the circuit’s electrical potentials. Choose a reference node, assign its voltage zero, and write KCL at the remaining unknown nodes. Ohm’s law expresses every resistor current using the voltages at its ends. This often avoids solving separately for every branch current.

rows: The chosen zero of potential; it need not represent a physical earth connection.
The potential at node $k$ relative to the reference node, positive at node $k$.
$G=\dfrac{1}{R}$, where $R$ is resistance; conductance is measured in siemens.
A group of non-reference nodes linked by ideal voltage sources, handled with boundary KCL and voltage constraints.

blocks.text: The current $i_{k\to j}$ is defined from node $k$ toward node $j$ through resistance $R_{kj}$. Voltages $v_k$ and $v_j$ use the same reference. The sum includes the resistor branches incident on node $k$; $I_{k,\mathrm{in}}$ is the net current injected into that node by current sources. A negative current means the actual direction opposes the chosen arrow.

steps.explanation: Choose resistor currents leaving the node as positive. An injected source current enters and therefore has the opposite sign.
Replace each resistor current with its voltage difference divided by resistance.
Collect the unknown voltages. For ordinary positive resistors, the diagonal coefficient sums incident conductances and each off-diagonal coefficient is the negative connecting conductance.

blocks.title: From KCL to the node-voltage equation

items: Choose a convenient reference, usually a node with many branches.
Label every non-reference voltage and mark voltages already fixed by sources.
Write KCL at unknown ordinary nodes and at supernode boundaries.
Write every voltage-source relation and dependent-source control relation.
Solve the simultaneous equations, then recover branch currents and powers.
Check KCL, source constraints, and total absorbed versus delivered power.

blocks.text: Node-voltage analysis also works for nonplanar circuits. The planarity check appearing in the lecture’s nodal procedure is unnecessary for this method; planarity is required for the mesh-current method. Never apply Ohm’s law to an ideal voltage source to guess its current.

blocks.prompt:
Use the node-voltage method to find $v_1$ and $v_2$.

```schematic
V1 0,3 -> 0,0 "$10\,\mathrm{V}$"
R1 0,3 -> 3,3 "$1\,\Omega$"
R2 3,3 -> 3,0 "$5\,\Omega$" v="$v_1$"
R3 3,3 -> 6,3 "$2\,\Omega$"
R4 6,3 -> 6,0 "$10\,\Omega$" v="$v_2$"
wire 6,3 -> 9,3
I1 9,0 -> 9,3 "$2\,\mathrm{A}$"
wire 9,0 -> 0,0
label 3,3 "1" above
label 6,3 "2" above
ground 3,0
```

steps.explanation: The source fixes vs=10 V; three resistor currents leave node 1.
The 2 A source injects current into node 2.
Multiply the KCL equations by 10 to remove fractions.
Substitute the second equation into the first.
These are voltages relative to ground.
The negative sign means current actually flows from node 2 toward node 1.

blocks.title: Two unknown node voltages (Lecture 3)

blocks.prompt:
Use the node-voltage method to find the branch currents $i_a$, $i_b$ and $i_c$.

```schematic
V1 0,3 -> 0,0 "$50\,\mathrm{V}$"
R1 0,3 -> 3,3 "$5\,\Omega$" i="$i_a$"
R2 3,3 -> 3,0 "$10\,\Omega$" i="$i_b$"

R3 6,3 -> 6,0 "$40\,\Omega$" i="$i_c$"

I1 9,0 -> 9,3 "$3\,\mathrm{A}$"
```

steps.explanation: Take the bottom wire as the reference. Only node $a$ is unknown; the $50\,\mathrm{V}$ source fixes the left end of the $5\,\Omega$ resistor. Sum the currents leaving $a$; the $3\,\mathrm{A}$ source enters it.
Multiply by 40 and solve.
Recover each branch current with Ohm's law, using its arrow.
Check KCL at $a$: $i_a$ plus the source current must leave through $i_b$ and $i_c$.

blocks.title: One node equation (Lecture 3)

blocks.text: Dependent sources: retain the control equation

A dependent source’s value must be solved with the rest of the circuit. Express its controlling current or voltage in the same node-voltage unknowns before substituting. For a current-controlled voltage source, the proportionality coefficient has units of ohms; for a voltage-controlled current source it has units of siemens.

Here $i_\Phi$ is the controlling current from $a$ to $b$, $R_{ab}$ is that resistor’s resistance, $v_c$ is the voltage of a dependent source whose negative terminal is grounded, and $r_m$ is its current-to-voltage coefficient in ohms. The signs must follow the control arrow and source polarity.

steps.explanation: KCL at node a.
KCL at b and the controlling-current relation.
Substitute the dependent-source value, then collect terms.
Elimination reduces the first equation to vb=10 V.
Recover the source control and check its prescribed value.
Resistor power is nonnegative under the passive sign convention.

blocks.title: Node voltages with a dependent source (Lecture 3)

blocks.text: Known voltages and supernodes

A voltage source connected to the reference node directly fixes the other node’s voltage, with the sign determined by its polarity. A source between two unknown non-reference nodes fixes only their voltage difference. Enclose those nodes and the source in a supernode, write KCL for currents crossing the boundary, and add the voltage constraint. Internal source current cancels from boundary KCL.

steps.explanation: The $100\,\mathrm{V}$ source sits between node 1 and the reference, so node 1 is known and needs no equation (special case 1).
Write KCL at node 2 only, with currents leaving; the $5\,\mathrm{A}$ source enters node 2.
Multiply by 50 and solve.

blocks.title: A voltage source to ground fixes a node (Lecture 3)

blocks.text: The source is positive at node $p$ and negative at node $q$, and $V_s$ is its voltage, independent or controlled. The boundary-current sum counts currents leaving the supernode, with entering currents negative. The two nodes remain distinct voltages; they are grouped only for KCL.

```schematic
R3 6,3 -> 6,0 "$50\,\Omega$"

R4 9,3 -> 9,0 "$100\,\Omega$"

I1 12,0 -> 12,3 "$4\,\mathrm{A}$"
wire 12,0 -> 0,0
label 3,3 "$a$" above
label 6,3 "$b$" below
label 9,3 "$c$" below
ground 3,0
```

steps.explanation: The grounded source fixes va. Keep the leftward controlling-current arrow.
Only branches crossing the b–c supernode boundary enter its KCL equation.
The dependent source supplies the missing voltage relation.
Substitute before solving.
The source voltage is 20 V, equal to 10 ohms times 2 A.

blocks.title: A supernode with a dependent source (Lecture 3)

blocks.text: Do not set the two supernode voltages equal. Do not include the internal voltage-source current in boundary KCL. A controlling current such as $\dfrac{v_b-v_a}{R}$ changes sign if you reverse its arrow.

Choose a reference that makes a voltage source directly set a node voltage when practical. Keep a small equation checklist: one KCL relation per unknown ordinary node or supernode, plus every source and control constraint.
Topic 3: Mesh-current method

For a planar circuit, assign one hypothetical circulating current to each mesh and write KVL around those meshes. A branch belonging to one mesh carries that mesh current. A branch shared by two meshes carries their algebraic combination. Assigning every mesh clockwise makes a shared resistor’s current a difference, which is easy to keep consistent.

rows: A chosen circulating current around mesh $k$; it is an analysis variable rather than necessarily a physical branch current.
The signed sum of the mesh currents crossing a branch; for two clockwise adjacent meshes it is their difference.
A combined KVL contour that bypasses a current-source branch shared by two meshes.
A source belonging to only one mesh; it fixes that mesh current directly.

blocks.text: Here $I_k$ and $I_\ell$ are clockwise currents in neighboring meshes. The shared branch current $i_{k\to\ell}$ and resistor voltage drop $v_R$ are referenced in mesh $k$’s traversal direction, and $R$ is the shared resistance. In mesh $\ell$’s KVL equation, the same drop is $R(I_\ell-I_k)$.

steps.explanation: Take clockwise currents IL and IR in the left and right windows. V1 is the left source voltage, V2 the right source voltage, R1 the left-top resistance, R2 the right-top resistance, and R3 the shared center-to-bottom resistance. Both sources are positive at their upper terminals. The left source is a rise.
Clockwise traversal through the right source goes from its positive terminal to its negative terminal, so it is a drop.
Collect terms. V1 fixes the left top node and V2 fixes the right top node relative to the common bottom node. R1 connects left to center, R2 center to right, and R3 center to bottom.
The lecture’s rightward top currents are i1 and i2; its downward center current is i3. Recover physical branch currents after solving.

blocks.text: KVL requires a consistent traversal direction and source polarity: traversing $-\to+$ is a rise, and $+\to-$ is a drop. Mesh currents can be negative; keep the original arrows and interpret the sign after solving. Check planarity before using meshes.

steps.explanation: KVL in the left mesh.
The center mesh shares the vertical resistors with its neighbors.
The right source is a drop in clockwise traversal.
Collect terms with currents in amperes.
Eliminate I1 and I3 from the center equation.
The right mesh’s actual circulation is counterclockwise.
The 8 ohm branch current is 3.6 A downward, not I1 alone.
For absorbed power, use current entering the positive source terminal. Both negative results mean delivery: 224 W and 16 W, respectively.

blocks.title: Three meshes (Lecture 3)

blocks.text: Mesh analysis with dependent sources

Express the controlling quantity using mesh currents before solving. A current through a shared resistor is a difference of mesh currents, so a source controlled by that current usually depends on two mesh unknowns. The control equation remains part of the system even if the dependent-source symbol lies in only one mesh.

```schematic
R4 0,5 -> 6,5 "$1\,\Omega$"

```

steps.explanation: Both lower meshes cross the 20 ohm resistor in opposite directions.
KVL in the lower-left mesh.
KVL in the upper triangular mesh.
KVL in the lower-right mesh includes the controlled-source drop.
Substitute the control relation into the third equation.
Solve the second equation for Ib, substitute into the third, and then recover Ib in terms of Ia.
Substitution into the first equation gives (125/74)Ia=50. Recover the other mesh currents and the control current.
The 4 ohm resistor’s physical current is the difference of the adjacent mesh currents.

blocks.title: Mesh currents with a dependent source (Lecture 3)

blocks.text: The controlling current gives a source voltage of $(15\,\Omega)(1.6\,\mathrm{A})=24\,\mathrm{V}$. Algebra verifies the original dependent circuit; circuit_validate and circuit_simulate with a fixed $24\,\mathrm{V}$ replacement reproduce the currents and $16\,\mathrm{W}$ result. This checks the operating point’s consistency rather than simulating the dependency directly.
Current sources and supermeshes

An ideal current source fixes current but leaves its voltage unknown. If it lies on the perimeter of one mesh, set that mesh current equal to the signed source current. If two meshes share it, combine their outer paths into a supermesh that bypasses the source branch. Write KVL around that combined path and add the source-current constraint.

The source current $I_s$ is positive in the shared-branch direction followed by mesh $a$, and opposed by mesh $b$. Reverse the sign if the arrow is reversed. A supermesh does not introduce a new independent current: $I_a$ and $I_b$ remain the unknowns.

```schematic
R1 0,6 -> 6,6 "$2\,\Omega$"

R3 3,3 -> 3,0 "$2\,\Omega$"

R4 6,0 -> 3,0 "$1\,\Omega$"

```

steps.explanation: The current source lies between the lower-left and upper meshes.
KVL around their combined boundary avoids the current-source branch.
KVL around the remaining right mesh.
The supermesh KVL, right-mesh KVL, and source constraint form a complete system.
Substitute the current constraint into both KVL equations and eliminate Ic.
The 1 ohm resistor belongs only to the right mesh. The result agrees with the source’s official solution.

blocks.title: A supermesh (Assessment AP 4.12)

blocks.text: A current source’s voltage is generally not zero. Do not write $RI$ for that voltage or drop its branch while forgetting the current constraint. If the source is dependent, add its control relation as well.
On a current-source perimeter, read the mesh current directly from the arrow. On a shared current-source branch, write the current-difference constraint first, then trace the supermesh boundary.
Practice problems

Try each problem before opening its solution. All node voltages use the stated ground, and all source powers use the passive sign convention (positive means absorbed). The textbook page images were inspected to transcribe the circuits; worked solutions below were derived independently. DC checks use circuit_validate and circuit_simulate. For the dependent source in P4.27, the simulation uses its solved voltage as a fixed source and the original control equation is checked separately.

blocks.answer: **Answers: (a) $11$; (b) $10$; (c) $11$; (d) $10$; (e) $5$; (f) $5$; (g) $7$.** These are dimensionless topology counts; no operating-point simulation is needed.

blocks.title: Textbook P4.1

steps.explanation: Choose nodal analysis because the two independent current sources enter KCL directly.
Multiply the first equation by $125$ and the second by $750$: $6v_1-5v_2=-300$ and $-30v_1+35v_2=2400$.
Multiply the first equation by $5$ and add: $10v_2=900$, so $v_2=90\,\mathrm{V}$. Back-substitution gives $6v_1=150$.

Check the connecting current: $\dfrac{25-90}{25}=-2.6\,\mathrm{A}$, so it flows toward $a$. The $3.2\,\mathrm{A}$ source delivers $288\,\mathrm{W}$; the $2.4\,\mathrm{A}$ source absorbs $60\,\mathrm{W}$; resistors absorb $228\,\mathrm{W}$. circuit_validate and circuit_simulate confirm the answers, KCL, and power balance.

blocks.answer: **$P_{2\Omega}=72\,\mathrm{W}$.** The currents and power agree with the official solution. circuit_validate and circuit_simulate confirm this result and the KCL and power balances.

blocks.prompt:
1. Use the mesh-current method to find $i_a$, $i_b$ and $i_c$.
2. Repeat with the polarity of the $64\,\mathrm{V}$ source reversed.

```schematic
V1 0,3 -> 0,0 "$40\,\mathrm{V}$"
R1 0,3 -> 3,3 "$3\,\Omega$" i="$i_a$"
R2 0,0 -> 3,0 "$2\,\Omega$"

R5 3,0 -> 6,0 "$1.5\,\Omega$"

```

steps.explanation: Choose clockwise mesh currents $I_L$ and $I_R$ in the left and right windows. Then $i_a=I_L$, $i_b=I_L-I_R$, and $i_c=-I_R$, since its arrow points leftward.
Left KVL gives $-40+(3+2)I_L+45(I_L-I_R)=0$, or $50I_L-45I_R=40$.
In part (a), clockwise traversal goes through the right source from negative to positive, so right KVL is $45(I_R-I_L)+(4+1.5)I_R-64=0$, or $-45I_L+50.5I_R=64$.
Substitute $I_L=\dfrac{40+45I_R}{50}$: $10I_R=100$. Thus $I_R=10\,\mathrm{A}$ and $I_L=9.8\,\mathrm{A}$.
In part (b), only the right equation’s source sign changes: $-45I_L+50.5I_R=-64$. Elimination gives $10I_R=-28$, so $I_R=-2.8\,\mathrm{A}$ and $I_L=-1.72\,\mathrm{A}$.

blocks.title: Textbook P4.37

steps.explanation: Treat $b$ and $c$ as a supernode, since an ideal voltage source connects them. Let their voltages be $v$ and $v_c$, and let $v_a$ denote node $a$’s voltage.
KCL at $a$: $\dfrac{v_a}{7.5}+\dfrac{v_a-v}{2.5}=4.8$, giving $v_a=9+0.75v$ when voltages are in volts.
Supernode KCL: $\dfrac{v-v_a}{2.5}+\dfrac{v}{10}+\dfrac{v_c}{2.5}+\dfrac{v_c-12}{1}=0$.
The controls are $i_x=\dfrac{v_a}{7.5}$ and $v_c-v=(1\,\Omega)i_x$. Hence, in SI numerical form, $v_c=v+\dfrac{v_a}{7.5}=1.1v+1.2$.
Substitution into boundary KCL gives $1.74v-13.92=0$.

Check the dependency: $v_c-v=2\,\mathrm{V}=(1\,\Omega)(2\,\mathrm{A})$. circuit_validate and circuit_simulate with a fixed $2\,\mathrm{V}$ replacement confirm the operating point and power balance. The dependent relation is verified algebraically because the simulator does not directly support controlled sources.

steps.explanation: A bridge network is a good nodal exercise because it cannot be reduced immediately by series/parallel combinations. Define $v_a,v_b,v_c$ relative to ground.
KCL: $\dfrac{v_a}{240}+\dfrac{v_a-v_b}{20}+\dfrac{v_a-v_c}{320}=1$; $\dfrac{v_b}{100}+\dfrac{v_b-v_a}{20}+\dfrac{v_b-v_c}{50}=0$; $\dfrac{v_c}{600}+\dfrac{v_c-v_b}{50}+\dfrac{v_c-v_a}{320}=0$.
The second equation gives $v_b=(\dfrac{5}{8})v_a+(\dfrac{1}{4})v_c$. Substitute into the third to obtain $v_c=(\dfrac{15}{19})v_a$, hence $v_b=(\dfrac{125}{152})v_a$.
Substitution into the first equation gives $v_a=72.96\,\mathrm{V}$, $v_b=60\,\mathrm{V}$, and $v_c=57.6\,\mathrm{V}$.
Recover $i_o=\dfrac{v_c}{600}$, $i_1=\dfrac{v_a-v_c}{320}$, and $i_2=\dfrac{v_b}{100}$.
The source current enters its negative-voltage terminal, so absorbed power is $p_s=-v_a(1\,\mathrm{A})=-72.96\,\mathrm{W}$.

blocks.prompt:
Use the mesh-current method to find the mesh currents $i_a$, $i_b$, $i_c$ (all clockwise) and the voltage $v$ across the current source.

```schematic
wire 0,3 -> 0,6
R1 0,6 -> 8,6 "$10\,\Omega$"
wire 8,6 -> 8,3
R2 0,3 -> 4,3 "$3\,\Omega$"
R3 4,3 -> 8,3 "$2\,\Omega$"
I1 4,0 -> 4,3 "$5\,\mathrm{A}$" v_rev="$v$"
V1 0,3 -> 0,0 "$100\,\mathrm{V}$"
V2 8,3 -> 8,0 "$50\,\mathrm{V}$"
R4 0,0 -> 4,0 "$6\,\Omega$"
R5 4,0 -> 8,0 "$4\,\Omega$"
```

steps.explanation: The current source is shared by the left and right lower meshes. Its upward arrow gives $I_c-I_a=5$.
Upper-mesh KVL: $10I_b+2(I_b-I_c)+3(I_b-I_a)=0$, or $15I_b-3I_a-2I_c=0$.
Bypass the source using the lower supermesh contour: $-100+3(I_a-I_b)+2(I_c-I_b)+50+4I_c+6I_a=0$, or $9I_a+6I_c-5I_b=50$.
Substitute $I_c=I_a+5$ into the upper equation to get $I_a=3I_b-2$. The supermesh becomes $15I_a-5I_b=20$, so $40I_b=50$.
From the left side, $v_b=100-3(I_a-I_b)=98.5\,\mathrm{V}$. The $6\,\Omega$ resistor carries $I_a$ from $e$ to $f$, so $v_e=6I_a=10.5\,\mathrm{V}$. Therefore $v=v_b-v_e$.

blocks.title: Lecture page 22: Shared current source

blocks.text: Summary

items: Identify electrical nodes before writing equations; ideal wires share one potential.
Distinguish branches, essential branches, loops, and meshes. Mesh analysis requires a planar circuit.
Node-voltage analysis uses KCL and resistor currents $\dfrac{v_k-v_j}{R}$; it works for planar and nonplanar circuits.
A grounded voltage source sets a known node voltage. A floating voltage source requires a supernode and a voltage-difference constraint.
Dependent sources need explicit control equations using the correct branch directions and units.
Mesh analysis uses KVL. A shared resistor carries a difference of adjacent clockwise mesh currents.
A perimeter current source fixes one mesh current; a shared source requires a supermesh and a current-difference constraint.
Recover requested branch quantities and check source constraints, KCL, and power balance. Negative current reverses the arrow; negative absorbed power means delivery.

blocks.text: Formula sheet

rows: Writing node-voltage equations or recovering currents.
Current injected by sources balances outgoing resistor currents.
The source’s negative terminal is the reference.
The source is positive at $p$, negative at $q$; pair with boundary KCL.
Both adjacent mesh currents are clockwise; the drop follows mesh $k$.
The shared source arrow follows mesh $a$ on that branch.
A connected circuit; $M$ is the mesh count when planar. Source constraints reduce ordinary unknown-current equations.
$r_m$ has units $\Omega$; $g_m$ has units $\mathrm{S}$. Retain control polarity and direction.
Use current entering the positive-voltage terminal for absorbed power.
